body: # Federal Open Market Committee. Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). The **Federal Open Market Committee** (**FOMC**) is a committee within the Federal Reserve System (colloquially "the Fed") that is charged under United States law with overseeing the nation's open market operations (e.g., the Fed's buying and selling of United States Treasury securities). Under the terms of the original Federal Reserve Act, each of the Federal Reserve banks were authorized to buy and sell in the open market bonds and short term obligations of the United States government, bank acceptances, cable transfers, and bills of exchange. The committee consists of the seven members of the Federal Reserve Board, the president of the New York Fed, and four of the other eleven regional Federal Reserve Bank presidents, serving one-year terms. All of the Reserve Bank presidents, even those who are not currently voting members of the FOMC, attend committee meetings, participate in discussions, and contribute to the committee's assessment of the economy and policy options.

# Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC): What It Is and Does. Image 7: Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC): The branch of the Federal Reserve System that determines the direction of monetary policy.:max_bytes(150000):strip_icc():format(webp)/Fomc_sketch_final-421f7e733967464fb52efd8ddf13ce6e.png). The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) directs open market operations (OMOs) in the United States. The committee is made up of 12 members, including seven members of the Board of Governors, the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and four of the remaining 11 Reserve Bank presidents who serve on a rotating basis. The FOMC is a branch of the Federal Reserve System that governs the country’s monetary policy. *   The Federal Open Market Committee determines the direction of monetary policy by directing open market operations. *   The committee is composed of the seven members of the Board of Governors and five Federal Reserve Bank presidents.
